common_name: Nadia Eggplant (Heat-Tolerant Glossy Italian Hybrid Eggplant)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Nadia is a vigorous, heat-tolerant hybrid that sets fruit reliably even in the hottest part of a Gulf South summer, when many eggplant varieties slow production.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm. Nadia is a widely grown hybrid eggplant producing glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit with tender, non-bitter flesh and few seeds, on a vigorous, high-yielding plant especially valued for continuing to set fruit through peak summer heat when many other eggplant varieties slow down. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm; dull, soft skin signals overripe fruit with more seeds and tougher flesh. Regular harvesting every few days keeps the plant productive over a long season, and staking helps support the heavy fruit load on the branches.

common_name: Long Red Slim Cayenne Pepper (Classic Slender Drying Cayenne)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Long Red Slim produces the classic thin, wrinkled, fiery red cayenne pods traditionally strung and dried for homemade cayenne pepper powder and pepper flakes.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Long Red Slim is a classic, widely grown cayenne cultivar producing narrow, tapering, thin-walled pods that ripen from green to bright red, packing substantial heat in a lightweight, easily dried pod. The thin walls make it ideal for stringing into traditional pepper ropes (ristras) or oven-drying and grinding into homemade cayenne powder or crushed red pepper flakes. Plants are productive over a long season and tolerate heat well, making cayenne one of the more reliable hot peppers for Gulf South summers; pick pods at full red color for maximum heat and flavor when drying.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

common_name: Tampiqueno Serrano Pepper (Classic Mexican Hot Serrano)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Tampiqueno is a classic serrano cultivar producing small, thin-walled, very hot pods used fresh in salsas and Mexican cooking.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Tampiqueno is a widely grown, classic serrano pepper cultivar producing small, slender, thin-walled pods that ripen from green to red, packing more heat than jalapeno in a smaller package, and used extensively fresh in salsas, pico de gallo, and other Mexican dishes where a bright, grassy heat is wanted. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season and tolerate heat well, making serrano peppers one of the more reliable hot pepper choices for Gulf South gardens. Harvest pods at any stage of ripeness, though full red pods have somewhat more sweetness alongside the heat.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Lunchbox is an AAS-winning series of compact plants producing abundant small, sweet, snack-sized peppers in red, orange, and yellow, perfect for eating whole straight from the garden.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Lunchbox is a popular sweet pepper series bred to produce large numbers of small, thin-walled, crunchy, sweet fruit about the size of a large grape or small egg, perfect for snacking whole, tossing into lunchboxes, or adding to salads without any need to slice. The compact, well-branched plants are productive over a long season and work well in both garden beds and containers. Harvest continuously as pods ripen to their full color (red, orange, or yellow depending on the specific variety) to keep the plant producing more fruit.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

common_name: Mad Hatter Pepper (Unique Flying-Saucer-Shaped Mild Pepper)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Mad Hatter produces distinctive flattened, lobed, flying-saucer-shaped pods with mild heat and a fruity, citrusy flavor, an AAS award-winning novelty pepper as much for its shape as its flavor.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Mad Hatter is an All-America Selections winner grown for its unusual, whimsical, flattened flying-saucer-shaped pods with distinctive lobed edges, a shape unlike almost any other common pepper, combined with a mild, sweet, subtly citrusy flavor reminiscent of its Capsicum baccatum relatives like aji peppers. It works well fresh in salads, pickled whole for a striking presentation, or lightly cooked, and the productive plants continue setting fruit over a long summer season. Harvest at any color stage from green to ripe yellow-orange, since the mild heat and flavor are enjoyable throughout ripening.
